record.paper_title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science
record.original_question: How are the organic molecules produced in Titan's atmosphere chemically altered after they reach the surface, including by hydrolysis during impact-induced melting, catalytic transformations, or other surface processes, and how do those altered products relate to Titan's surface composition, dunes, and prebiotic chemistry?

evidence.quote: 10) How are molecules produced in Titan’s atmosphere altered on the surface?

Titan’s atmosphere produces a wide variety of organic molecules (Yung et al., 1984; Waite et al., 2005, 2007; Vuitton et al., 2019) which condense in the lower stratosphere and accumulate on the surface.

Moreover, molecules produced in the atmosphere may also be altered once on the surface, e.g. by hydrolysis during episodic melting induced by impacts (Neish et al., 2008, 2009, 2010; Poch et al., 2012; Cleaves II et al., 2014; Crósta et al., 2021) - see also Chapter 13.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, possesses a dense N2/CH4 atmosphere in which photochemistry produces a diverse inventory of organic molecules (e.g., hydrocarbons, nitriles, and heavier macromolecular "tholin"-like solids). These species condense in the lower stratosphere and accumulate on Titan's surface, where they may be incorporated into dune fields, mid-latitude plains, lake/sea sediments, and impact ejecta. Once deposited, these organics can in principle undergo further chemical transformation through processes such as: (i) hydrolysis in transient liquid water produced by impact-induced melting of the H2O-ice crust (with characteristic cooling timescales of 10^2–10^4 years for kilometer-scale craters); (ii) heterogeneous catalysis on mineral or ice substrates; (iii) cryogenic solid-state chemistry; (iv) interaction with cryovolcanic fluids or aqueous ammonia brines; and (v) radiolysis driven by galactic cosmic rays penetrating the upper meters of the surface.

Provide a quantitative, mechanistic characterization of the post-deposition chemical evolution of atmospherically produced organics on Titan's surface. Specifically:

(a) Identify the dominant alteration pathways (hydrolysis, catalysis, radiolysis, thermal processing, other) as a function of latitude, geological setting (dunes, plains, craters, lakes), and time, and determine the resulting product distributions, including yields of amino acids, nucleobase analogues, urea, carboxylic acids, and other prebiotically relevant species from the hydrolysis of nitrile-bearing precursors such as HCN polymers, HC3N, and tholins.

(b) Quantify the mass and compositional fluxes linking atmospheric production rates to the present-day surface inventory, accounting for burial, lateral transport by aeolian and fluvial processes, and chemical conversion.

(c) Determine how these altered products contribute to the observed spectral and compositional properties of Titan's dunes and equatorial plains, and to the composition of any subsurface aqueous reservoirs in which prebiotic chemistry could proceed.

The problem is to construct and validate a predictive surface-chemistry model that resolves (a)–(c) against laboratory analog data and Cassini/Huygens and forthcoming in situ observational constraints.
artifact.status_search_result: The chemical alteration of Titan's atmospherically derived organics on the surface remains an open research problem in planetary science. Laboratory studies of impact-induced hydrolysis of tholins (Neish et al., Poch et al., Cleaves et al.) demonstrate that biologically relevant molecules (amino acids, nucleobases) can form, but the global-scale pathways, rates, and surface inventories are unresolved and motivate the upcoming Dragonfly mission (planned arrival ~2034) which is specifically designed to address surface composition and prebiotic chemistry on Titan.

status_evidence.title: Dragonfly mission overview
status_evidence.snippet: Dragonfly is a NASA mission to send a rotorcraft to Titan to investigate prebiotic chemistry and habitability of dozens of sites.
status_evidence.claim: Surface organic chemistry on Titan is an open question targeted by a future in situ mission.

status_evidence.title: Neish et al., hydrolysis of Titan tholins
status_evidence.snippet: Laboratory hydrolysis of Titan tholins yields amino acids on timescales relevant to impact melt pools.
status_evidence.claim: Hydrolysis of atmospherically produced organics is mechanistically demonstrated but globally unconstrained.
